summary: Learners classify elements as metals or non-metals from a cluster of co-occurring property evidence (conductivity, malleability, lustre, oxide acidity), link that classification to periodic-table position (metals left/centre, non-metals upper right with a staircase boundary), and state a chemical difference (metal oxides tend to be basic, non-metal oxides tend to be acidic). Exceptions (liquid mercury, conducting graphite, metalloids) teach that the divide is a strong tendency, not an absolute rule. Age 11–13.
misconceptions: All metals are magnetic (only iron/nickel/cobalt are).
All metals are hard and solid (mercury is liquid; some are soft).
Any shiny material is a metal (lustre alone is not sufficient).
Metal and non-metal oxides behave the same in water (they differ in acidity).

activities.title: Test-and-sort bench: metal or not?
steps: Take each solid element sample and run quick tests: touch it to a circuit (does the bulb light?), tap it with a hammer (does it flatten or shatter?), and check its shine (lustrous or dull?). Then, for elements whose oxide dissolves in water, test a simulated or teacher-prepared oxide solution with universal indicator (acidic or basic?). Mercury is only simulated or shown by the teacher in a sealed sample, never hammered or burned.
Record each result in a results table, one row per element.
As evidence accumulates, place each sample onto a metal or non-metal map overlaid on the periodic table, and watch where the two clusters land.
Work through puzzle cases — liquid mercury and conducting graphite — and decide how to classify them despite one odd property.
State one chemical difference between the two classes: metal oxides tend to be basic/alkaline, non-metal oxides tend to be acidic (a strong pattern, not a guarantee for every oxide).
activities.insight: Metals and non-metals are distinguished by a CLUSTER of co-occurring properties, not one trait. The shiny, malleable, conducting, basic-oxide elements pool on the left/centre of the periodic table and the dull, brittle, insulating, acidic-oxide elements on the upper right. The staircase divide broadly matches the metal/non-metal split, with metalloids along it and hydrogen (a non-metal placed top left) as a notable exception.

activities.title: Shaded periodic table reference
steps: Study a periodic table shaded by the metal/non-metal divide, with the staircase boundary and metalloids straddling it marked.
Use a tap-to-reveal comparison chart with a metals column and a non-metals column; tap a property (e.g. malleability, conductivity, oxide acidity) to highlight which side shows it.
Given a new element's position, predict whether it is likely a metal or non-metal and which properties you'd expect.
activities.insight: Periodic-table position predicts metal/non-metal character and its associated property cluster; the boundary is a staircase with metalloids in between, so it is a graded divide rather than a hard line.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: does a magnet define a metal?
steps: Lay out copper, aluminium, iron and a shiny plastic strip; the teacher presents a sealed/demonstrated sample of liquid mercury (never pupil-handled). Before testing, predict which a magnet will pick up and explain WHY.
Test with a magnet and observe: only the iron sticks (copper, aluminium and mercury do not, and the plastic is not a metal).
Explain the gap between prediction and result, then give two other tests (conductivity, malleability) that show copper IS a metal despite not being magnetic.
Decide whether the demonstrated liquid mercury is a metal, and whether a shiny sweet wrapper is really metal or just shiny plastic, saying which test settles each.

Answer: where on the periodic table would you look to predict whether an element is a metal, and why are metals chosen for saucepan bases versus electrical wires — which property does the work each time?
activities.insight: Magnetism and shine are single misleading cues; metals are identified by a coherent cluster (conductivity, malleability where state allows, lustre, mostly high melting points, left/centre periodic position). Only iron, nickel and cobalt are commonly magnetic; shiny plastic is not a metal; and liquid mercury is still a metal.

checkQuestion: A friend says 'you can always tell a metal because it's shiny and a magnet sticks to it.' I show you mercury (a shiny liquid metal), copper (a metal a magnet does NOT stick to), and a shiny plastic gift bag. Is your friend's rule right? Then the important part: explain what really makes something a metal.
checkAnswer: The rule is wrong. Most magnets only stick to iron, nickel and cobalt — most metals (copper, gold, aluminium) aren't magnetic — and shininess alone isn't enough (shiny plastic isn't a metal; mercury is a liquid metal). Metals are better identified by a CLUSTER of properties: good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable/ductile, lustrous, mostly high melting points, and their position on the left/centre of the periodic table. Full marks reject 'magnetic = metal' and give conduction/malleability.
